messages.content:
Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a post about why a company is investing in developer relations. Around 250 words.

output:
Investing in developer relations, for a while, meant sponsoring a conference booth and calling it done. That's not what we're doing.

We're hiring three developer advocates this quarter and giving them a mandate: spend most of their time writing code, not slides. Their first job is to ship sample apps and open-source integrations that solve problems our own users hit last month — the kind of work that used to sit in a backlog because no team owned it.

The push started with a support ticket pattern. Forty-one developers asked the same question about our webhook retry logic in Q2, and the answer lived in a Slack thread, not our docs. A developer relations team fixes that gap by writing the docs, filing the API issue, and telling the platform team which error messages actually confuse people.

We measured what happens when a company skips this. Our churn data shows accounts that never talk to a human before month three cancel at twice the rate of accounts that do. A GitHub issue answered within a day, a Discord question resolved before a Monday deploy — these keep people building instead of switching to a competitor with better docs.

The team reports to product, not marketing. That's the part worth stating plainly: their job is to change what we build, based on what they hear, not to generate leads. Success for them next year looks like a lower number of "how do I" support tickets and a shorter time from signup to first working integration.

We're publishing the team's roadmap on GitHub next week so anyone can see what they're working on and file requests directly.
